title: Explain the key components of a microservices architecture (API Gateway, Service Registry, Config Server, inter-service communication, DB-per-service, load balancer, monitoring/logging, circuit breaker).
shortTitle: Key components of a microservices architecture
keyPoints: API Gateway is the single entry point handling routing, authentication, and rate limiting for all client requests.
Service Registry (Eureka or Consul) lets services find each other by logical name instead of hardcoded IP addresses.
Config Server centralizes externalized configuration so services read settings from one place without redeployment.
Inter-service communication is synchronous (REST, Feign, gRPC) or asynchronous (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
Database-per-service gives each service a private data store so schemas evolve independently.
Circuit breakers (Resilience4j) stop cascading failures by failing fast when a dependency is unhealthy.
Observability (Prometheus, Grafana, ELK, Zipkin) provides metrics, logs, and distributed tracing across all services.

s1_definition.oneliner: Gateway is the front door, Registry is the directory, Config Server is the rulebook, load balancer spreads traffic, each service owns its DB, Kafka and REST connect them, and monitoring plus circuit breakers keep it alive.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **API Gateway** – the single entry point that handles routing, authentication, and rate limiting so clients never talk to services directly.
- **Service Registry** – a directory (Eureka or Consul) where services register under a logical name and callers resolve that name instead of hardcoding addresses.
- **Config Server** – centralizes externalized configuration so you change a timeout once without rebuilding any service.
- **Inter-service communication** – synchronous (REST, Feign, gRPC) when the caller needs an answer, asynchronous (Kafka, RabbitMQ) when it should not wait.
- **Database-per-service** – each service owns a private data store; no other service touches its tables.
- **Circuit breaker** – wraps remote calls and fails fast when a dependency is unhealthy, stopping cascading failures.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a large campus. The API Gateway is the main reception that checks your ID and directs you. The Service Registry is the campus directory that tells reception which building the Payment department is in today, because departments move. The Config Server is the central rulebook every department reads from. The load balancer is the queue manager sending you to whichever teller counter is free. Monitoring is the CCTV and alarm room. The circuit breaker is the "counter temporarily closed" sign so customers do not pile up at a desk that cannot help them.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A microservices architecture is assembled from a standard set of components, and in interviews I describe each by the problem it solves. The API Gateway is the single public entry point that handles routing, authentication, and rate limiting so these cross-cutting concerns live in one place instead of being copied into every service. The Service Registry solves the problem that instances come and go with scaling and deploys. The Config Server centralizes externalized configuration, and inter-service communication comes in two flavors: synchronous with REST or Feign when the caller needs an answer, and asynchronous with Kafka when it should not wait.

Database-per-service keeps each service's data private, so the Payment Service at National Bank of India never reaches into the Account Service's tables. A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy instances, and circuit breakers in Resilience4j fail fast so one slow dependency does not take the whole system down. Observability ties everything together with Prometheus for metrics, ELK for structured logs, and Zipkin with a shared traceId so Pankaj can follow one of Rajesh's transfers across the gateway, payment, and account services.

The point I always make to an interviewer is that none of these are optional luxuries. Without a registry you get brittle addresses, without a config server you get config drift, and without circuit breakers one failing dependency cascades into a full outage.

Remember one sentence: a production microservices architecture needs an API Gateway for routing, a Service Registry for discovery, a Config Server for configuration, circuit breakers for resilience, and observability for tracing, and none of them are optional.
